claims.text: Little's law: the average number of requests in flight equals throughput times the average time each spends in the system, over the same period (long-run averages of a stable system). Illustration: 10 in flight / 0.02 s = 500 per second.
claims.source_hint: content/glossary.yaml littles-law; any operations-research reference for Little's law (L = lambda W)

claims.text: Below a full shared resource the average time changes little, so throughput rises roughly with in flight (ideal case). Once a resource or a limit like catalog-reads is full, throughput stops rising; by Little's law more in flight means a longer average. Checks: rate40 < 20 x rate1, p95 rises.
claims.source_hint: reasoning from Little's law; scripts/backend/load-steps.sh lines 39-48 checks; outputs/stage-4/scripts/backend/load-steps.txt @ stage-4

claims.text: catalog-reads: PermitLimit = 20, QueueLimit = 5, bindable from RateLimiting:CatalogReads; docker-compose.yml sets no such value; it checks every read, and one beyond running + waiting gets 503 at once. At 20 and 40 in flight at most 20 run at once, so 200/s at 40 cannot be twice that at 20.
claims.source_hint: DonHang.Api/Program.cs lines 143-148, 162-181; docker-compose.yml; ProductsController.cs line 24 @ stage-4

claims.text: The ASP.NET Core concurrency limiter counts permits and queue in memory of one app process, so each api process has its own 20 + 5; the lab runs one api container.

claims.text: curl keeps up to n reads in flight, as the script comment (lines 16-18) says; the Little's law check passing at every step confirms the average in flight stayed close to n. No curl behaviour is described beyond the comment (curl has no versions.yaml key).

awk reads each curl line ($1 status, $2 time, NR = answers), counts 200 and 503, average, p95 (lines sorted by time first, element at NR*0.95 rounded), 200/s over the step's elapsed time, and NR/wall*avg (every status) as the Little's law column.

Final checks: product within 0.7n..1.3n at each step; p95 at 40 > at 1; 200/s at 40 < 20 x 200/s at 1; no 503 at 1-20; some 503 at 40. Captured output masks the numbers; all five check lines read yes.
slo.md is where Đơn Hàng writes its SLIs; S3 (product reads) counts the 503 of the catalog-reads limit as bad, so a load test against the live api spends error budget.
Rate limiting: the fixed-window orders limit refuses with 429 and Retry-After; the concurrency limiter's refusals stay 503.

The lab runs every service (curl in the lab container, Caddy as reverse proxy in front of the api, api, PostgreSQL) on one machine, so its numbers show the curve's shape, not production's capacity; deciding capacity needs an environment shaped like production.

claims.text: Trade-offs: a burst gives a quick sign but no curve; fixed steps show the ceiling but take longer; lab is cheap and repeatable but not production's numbers; a production-shaped environment gives sizing numbers at a cost.

Each list read queries PostgreSQL (CatalogService.ListAsync, no cache), whose connections orders also use; the script does not show whether they fill before the 20 permits. If throughput stopped rising before 20, more permits only add waiting reads; test the live api only when agreed.
